HLD: Delayed Trigger Service

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Intermediate–Advanced Prerequisites:Message Queues and Leader Election

TL;DR

A service that fires HTTP callbacks at a future time. Short delays (≤15 min) go directly to a queue. Long delays park in a database and a sweeper migrates them to the queue as their fire time approaches.

In 3 sentences: Services register “call me back in X minutes” requests. The system persists the trigger durably, then fires the HTTP callback at the right time with retries. Two tiers: short delays use a managed queue (SQS); long delays sit in a database until a sweeper promotes them.

1. Understanding the Problem

A delayed trigger service lets internal services register a callback with a future fire time (e.g., “ping me back in 30 minutes”). When the delay elapses, the service POSTs a response to a callback URL the caller provided. It’s the building block behind reminders, payment retries, abandoned-cart nudges, “release the seat hold in 7 minutes,” and “auto-cancel the order if not paid in 15 min.”

2. Naive First Cut

Why this breaks under real constraints:

  • Process crash loses every pending trigger - no durability. If the box reboots, every “fire in 10 min” is gone.
  • One JVM caps throughput - ScheduledExecutorService is fine for thousands of timers, hopeless at millions.
  • No horizontal scale - two replicas would each fire the callback, giving duplicates.
  • No retry on callback failure - if the caller’s endpoint is down at fire time, the trigger is silently lost.
  • No long delays - JVM heap pressure with millions of DelayedTask objects.
  • Hot fire-time spikes - “fire at top of the hour” thundering herd would saturate the executor.💡 A thundering herd is a crowd of work arriving in the same instant rather than spread out. Here it happens because humans and cron jobs ask for round delays, so an enormous share of triggers all come due exactly on the minute. Learn more →

The rest of the doc evolves this into a durable, sharded, bucketed scheduler with a timing-wheel front end and at-least-once HTTP callback delivery.

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • Airbnb Dynein - short-delay jobs (≤15 min) go straight to SQS; long-delay jobs sit in DynamoDB and a sweeper moves them to SQS as fire time approaches. We borrow this two-tier split.
  • Apache Kafka Purgatory + Hierarchical Timing Wheels - O(1) insert/expire for millions of in-memory timers across multiple resolutions. We use this for the hot, near-future tier.
  • AWS SQS delay queues - built-in 0–15 min delay primitive. We treat SQS as the “execution lane” once a trigger is within 15 min.
  • Stripe Idempotency-Key - caller-supplied idempotency key on register so repeated submissions don’t create duplicate triggers.
  • Netflix Maestro - sharded execution layer; we use the same partition-by-triggerId model so each shard is independently leader-led.

When deep dives below cite “borrowing from Dynein” or “borrowing from Kafka Purgatory,” that’s what they mean.

4. Functional Requirements

Core:

  1. registerTrigger(callerId, callbackUrl, payload, delaySeconds, idempotencyKey) returns a triggerId. Persists the intent durably.
  2. At now + delaySeconds, the service POSTs {triggerId, payload} to callbackUrl and considers the trigger fired only after a 2xx ack.
  3. cancelTrigger(triggerId) - best-effort cancel before fire time.

Below the line (out of scope for the interview):

  • Recurring / cron-like triggers.
  • Workflow chaining (trigger A fires trigger B).
  • Per-caller priority / rate limits beyond fairness.
  • Cross-region active-active.

5. Non-Functional Requirements

Core:

  • Durability - once register returns 200, the trigger must fire even if every component crashes. No silent drops.
  • On-time firing - P99 jitter < 1s for short delays, < 5s for long (>15 min) delays.💡 Jitter here means “how far off the requested time we actually fire”. P99 is the figure 99% of fires stay inside, so this says the worst 1 in 100 triggers may be up to a second late - not the average. Learn more →
  • Throughput - 10K registers/sec and 10K fires/sec at peak. In steady state those two have to be equal, so one number drives both.
  • At-least-once + idempotent - callback may fire twice; caller must dedupe via triggerId.💡 At-least-once delivery = we promise never to drop a callback, and in exchange we may send it twice. The alternative, exactly-once, cannot be built over a network that loses acknowledgements, so the duplicate is pushed onto the caller to recognise. Learn more →

Below the line: strict-once delivery, sub-millisecond jitter, multi-region failover.

6. Scale Estimation (Back-of-Envelope)

  • Pending set: 50M triggers in flight at any given time across all callers
  • Write QPS: 10K registers/sec at peak.💡 QPS = queries per second, the rate of requests arriving. Learn more → Cross-check against the pending set: 50M pending at 10K fires/sec implies an average delay of ~5,000s, call it 83 minutes. That matches the workload - seat holds, payment timeouts, nudges - and tells us the long tail is a minority of rows, not the bulk.
  • Read QPS: the sweeper reads a handful of partitions per second (the sub-shards of the bucket currently in range), plus ~5K status queries/sec from callers
  • Storage: the live table is small - 50M rows at ~500B is ~25GB. The volume is in fired rows: 10K/sec is 864M/day, so a 30-day audit retention is ~13TB. That is the number that decides whether audit history lives in Cassandra or gets shipped to object storage.
  • Timing precision: < 1s P99 jitter for short delays, which is the constraint that rules out a plain minute-granularity poll

7. Core Entities

  • Trigger - id, callerId, callbackUrl, payload, fireAt, status (PENDING / IN_FLIGHT / FIRED / FAILED / CANCELLED), attemptCount.
  • Caller - registered service with auth credentials and (optionally) per-tenant rate limits.
  • Bucket - a 1-minute window keyed by floor(fireAt). Triggers live in their bucket’s row in Cassandra.
  • Dispatcher - worker that turns “trigger is due” into “HTTP POST to callbackUrl.”
  • Sweeper - process that scans upcoming buckets and pushes due-soon triggers into the in-memory wheel.

8. API / System Interface

POST /v1/triggers
Authorization: Bearer <caller JWT>
Idempotency-Key: <client-supplied uuid>

{
  "callbackUrl": "https://orders.internal/seat-hold/expire",
  "payload":     {"holdId": "h_8c4"},
  "delaySeconds": 420
}
HTTP
200 OK
{ "triggerId": "trg_01HZ...", "fireAt": "2026-06-12T14:31:00Z" }
HTTP
DELETE /v1/triggers/{triggerId}
Authorization: Bearer <caller JWT>
HTTP

The dispatcher fires this against the caller:

POST <callbackUrl>
X-Trigger-Id: trg_01HZ...
X-Trigger-Attempt: 1

{ "triggerId": "trg_01HZ...", "payload": {"holdId": "h_8c4"} }
HTTP

Caller responds 2xx for ack. Anything else (or timeout) → retry with exponential backoff, eventually a dead-letter queue (DLQ).💡 Exponential backoff means each retry waits longer than the last, so a struggling endpoint is not hammered. A dead-letter queue is where a message goes once retries are exhausted - a parking area a human can inspect, instead of either dropping the work or retrying it forever.

Security notes: caller authenticated via short-lived JSON Web Token (JWT) minted for the service identity; callbackUrl validated against an allow-list of registered base URLs per caller (prevents using us as a server-side request forgery (SSRF) springboard). payload size capped at 4 KB.💡 A JWT is a signed token proving which service is calling. SSRF is the attack where someone persuades your server to make an HTTP request on their behalf - and a service whose entire job is “POST to a URL I give you” is the perfect springboard for it, hence the allow-list. Learn more →

9. High-Level Design

We’ll layer in components as the three FRs demand them.

FR1: Register a trigger

New components we need:

  1. Trigger API - the HTTP service callers hit to register or cancel triggers. Validates the request and writes the row.
  2. Cassandra (partitioned by fire-time bucket) - durable storage for all triggers. Partitioned by the 1-minute window containing fireAt, so the sweeper can ask “give me all triggers due in minute M” with one partition read.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Caller (e.g., the Order Service) calls POST /v1/triggers with a callback URL and delaySeconds: 420 (7 minutes) → “Call me back in 7 minutes to expire this seat hold”
  2. API computes fireAt = now + 420s, generates a unique ULID triggerId, and writes the row to Cassandra.💡 A ULID is an id that is unique without asking any central service for it, and whose text form sorts by creation time. Both properties matter here: no coordination on the write path, and ids that cluster by time in the store. Learn more → The partition key is the 1-minute bucket containing fireAt (e.g., 14:31) - this groups triggers by fire time for efficient sweeping later
  3. Returns 200 OK with the triggerId and exact fireAt timestamp once Cassandra acks at QUORUM💡 A quorum write means a majority of the copies of that row confirmed it before we answer the caller. That is what lets us promise durability in the requirements: losing one machine cannot lose the trigger. Learn more →

Why partition by 1-minute buckets? The sweeper needs to find “all triggers about to fire” without scanning. One partition read per minute is a single seek. This is the one structural decision FR1 has to get right, because every other component reads through it.

What FR1 leaves broken: the write is durable, which is the headline requirement, and that is genuinely all it is. The Idempotency-Key header in the API contract above is accepted and ignored – a caller whose connection drops and retries gets two rows, two triggerIds, and two callbacks seven minutes later. Our own retries are no better: nothing at fire time can tell “this trigger has not fired” from “this trigger fired and we lost the ack.” Deep Dive 2 handles both ends.

FR2: Fire the callback at the right time

A trigger is due when fireAt <= now, and FR1 already grouped triggers by the minute they are due in. So the simplest firing mechanism is a loop: read the bucket that is currently in range, hand whatever is due to something that can make an HTTP call, repeat.

New components we need (in addition to the ones above):

  1. Sweeper (leader-elected, per shard) - every second, reads the bucket covering now and enqueues any trigger whose fireAt has passed.💡 Leader election ensures only one sweeper owns each shard - without it, two sweepers would enqueue the same bucket. Learn more →
  2. SQS - the handoff between “this is due” and “someone is calling the callback.” Decouples the sweeper’s scan rate from the dispatcher pool’s throughput.
  3. Dispatcher Pool - workers that pull from SQS, read the trigger from Cassandra, and POST the callback to the caller’s URL. Stateless; scales horizontally.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Sweeper runs per shard, leader-elected via ZooKeeper/etcd. Once a second it reads the partition for the current minute bucket
  2. For every row in that partition with fireAt <= now and status = PENDING, it pushes the triggerId to SQS. The loop has to run at least this often: a minute-granularity sweep would miss fireAt by up to 60 seconds
  3. Dispatcher pulls from SQS, reads the current trigger row from Cassandra, and POSTs the payload to the callback URL
  4. On 2xx → dispatcher writes status = FIRED to Cassandra and deletes the SQS message
  5. On non-2xx or timeout → requeue to SQS with exponential backoff (10s → 30s → 2min → 10min → 30min). After N attempts, stop retrying
  6. If the dispatcher crashes after the POST but before deleting from SQS → the visibility timeout expires, another dispatcher picks it up and retries. At-least-once is the contract💡 A visibility timeout is the window during which a queue hides a message it has handed to one worker. Delete it inside the window and it is done; stay silent and the queue assumes the worker died and gives the message to someone else. That mechanism is exactly why duplicates are possible.

Why does the dispatcher read Cassandra before firing? The SQS message holds only the triggerId, to keep messages small and to force the dispatcher to read current state rather than a snapshot from whenever the sweeper ran.

What FR2 leaves broken: this fires triggers correctly and then falls over on four separate things, all of them load-shaped rather than logic-shaped.

  • The jitter target is only just met, and only when nothing is wrong. A one-second loop means a trigger can wait up to a second before the sweeper even notices it, and the Cassandra read plus the SQS round-trip land on top of that. P99 jitter < 1s has no headroom at all.
  • Every bucket is one Cassandra partition, and fire times are not uniform. Callers ask for round delays from crons that themselves run on the minute, so 14:00:00 collects a few million triggers while 14:00:37 collects a few thousand. That is a hot partition, the sweeper’s read of it takes seconds instead of milliseconds, and the triggers inside it all land in SQS in one burst.💡 A hot partition is one slice of the data that holds or receives far more than its share. The cluster may be mostly idle while the single machine owning that slice is overwhelmed, so extra capacity does not help until the slice itself is split. Learn more → Deep Dive 1 takes both of these.
  • Long delays make the sweeper do pointless work. A 30-day horizon is 43,200 minute-buckets. The sweeper only ever reads the current one, so that part is fine – but nothing ever ages a fired row out, and a 30-day trigger’s row sits in the hot table for 30 days competing with the rows that matter. Deep Dive 3.
  • One slow caller takes down every caller. The dispatcher POST is a blocking call against somebody else’s endpoint. A caller whose URL hangs for its full 60-second timeout occupies a dispatcher for 60 seconds, and there is nothing partitioning the pool. Deep Dive 4.
  • Cancel is still racy. FR3 is next and will set a status flag, but the dispatcher above reads that flag when it dequeues, not when it fires. Deep Dive 5.

FR3: Cancel a trigger

New components we need: None! Cancellation reuses existing infrastructure - it just flips a status flag in Cassandra that the dispatcher checks at fire time.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Caller hits DELETE /v1/triggers/{triggerId} → API sets status = CANCELLED in Cassandra (only if current status is PENDING)
  2. We DON’T try to remove the trigger from SQS - that’s too racy and SQS doesn’t support targeted deletion by content
  3. The dispatcher reads the row when it dequeues the message, sees CANCELLED, and drops it without firing the callback
  4. This is “lazy cancel”: the cancel is durable instantly, but the trigger message may sit in the queue until its fire time before being discarded

Why not remove from the queue immediately? SQS doesn’t support “find and delete message with triggerId X.” And even if it did, the message might be in flight to a dispatcher at the exact moment the cancel arrives. The flag in Cassandra is the single source of truth and the dispatcher checks it before firing.

What FR3 leaves broken: “the dispatcher checks it before firing” is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and it is not true in the way it sounds. The dispatcher reads status at dequeue, and SQS hands it the message with some slack before fireAt, so there is a window – read PENDING at T-3s, POST at T+0, cancel arrived at T-2s and was durably committed and still the callback fires. The caller did everything right and got called anyway. Deep Dive 5 moves the read to the one point where it can actually be decisive.

10. Technology Choices

Tier / Purpose What it stores Access pattern Primary pick Alternatives
OLTP trigger store triggerId, callerId, callbackUrl, fireAt, payload, status, idempotencyKey write-heavy on register, point read on fire, range scan by fireAt bucket Cassandra / DynamoDB (partition key = bucket) ScyllaDB, Bigtable
Short-delay execution lane trigger envelope, retries metadata FIFO with per-msg delay 0–15 min SQS (delay queue) RabbitMQ delayed exchange, Redis Streams + ZSET
In-memory timer wheel next-tick triggers per shard O(1) insert/expire hierarchical timing wheel in-process Netty HashedWheelTimer, Redis sorted set per bucket
Long-delay sweep index fireAt bucket (1-min) → list of triggerIds range scan by upcoming bucket secondary index on Cassandra (partition = bucket minute) DynamoDB GSI on fireAtMinute
Idempotency cache (callerId, idempotencyKey) → triggerId TTL’d KV Redis with TTL = max delay + grace DynamoDB with TTL
Audit / DLQ failed callbacks after N retries append-only Kafka topic + S3 sink Kinesis Firehose
scroll →

Two non-obvious picks worth a note:

Why Cassandra for the trigger store, not Postgres. Writes dominate (every register is a write, every fire is an update). The access pattern is partition key = fireAt-bucket → range scan within the bucket. That’s exactly what wide-column stores are built for. Postgres would work but you’d be hand-rolling sharding and the time-series indexing.

Why a separate timing wheel in-process when the queue already has delay. SQS caps at 15-minute delay, and even within that window, draining millions of messages at the exact same fireAt second is hard to control. The timing wheel gives precise local scheduling and feeds SQS only with messages that are due in the next few seconds. Deep Dive 1 is where this gets earned – the high-level design above deliberately goes without it.

11. Data Modeling

Cassandra / DynamoDB (Trigger Store — durable trigger records):

Table: triggers
  PK: fire_at_bucket (minute-granularity timestamp, e.g., "2026-07-15T14:30")
  SK: trigger_id (UUID)
  Columns: caller_id, callback_url, payload (JSON), fire_at (exact timestamp),
           status (PENDING/IN_FLIGHT/FIRED/FAILED/CANCELLED), attempt_count,
           idempotency_key, created_at

Table: trigger_by_id (for point lookups and cancellation)
  PK: trigger_id
  Columns: fire_at_bucket, caller_id, status, callback_url

Redis (Idempotency Cache + Short-Delay Queue):

-- Idempotency dedup
Key: "idem:{callerId}:{idempotencyKey}" → trigger_id
TTL: max_delay + 24 hours

-- Upcoming triggers (next 60 seconds worth)
Key: "triggers:due:{shard_id}" → Sorted Set (score = fire_at_unix_ms, member = trigger_id)

In-Process Timing Wheel (Precise Firing):

Structure: Hierarchical timing wheel
  Wheel levels: [1s slots × 60] → [1min slots × 60] → [1hr slots × 24]
  Each slot: linked list of trigger_ids to fire at that tick
  Resolution: 100ms per tick
  Capacity: 1M pending triggers per worker in ~200MB RAM

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Register trigger Cassandra INSERT INTO triggers at the correct bucket + INSERT INTO trigger_by_id
Cancel trigger Cassandra + Redis Update status=CANCELLED in Cassandra, add to Redis cancel set
Sweep upcoming triggers Cassandra Range scan: SELECT * FROM triggers WHERE fire_at_bucket = {next_minute} AND status = 'PENDING'
Fire trigger (on time) Timing wheel → HTTP POST Tick fires → pop trigger_id → check cancel set → POST to callback_url
Retry failed trigger Kafka DLQ → Worker Exponential backoff: 1s, 5s, 30s, 5min. After 5 failures → move to DLQ
scroll →

How a Trigger Fires Exactly On Time (Within 1s Jitter):

  1. Trigger registered: fire_at = now() + 3 hours → stored in Cassandra bucket 14:30 with status=PENDING
  2. Sweeper runs every minute: at 14:29 it scans bucket 14:30 and loads all due triggers
  3. Pushes each trigger_id into the in-process timing wheel at the exact second slot
  4. At 14:30:00.000 — timing wheel tick fires → pops trigger_ids due at this second
  5. For each: check Redis cancel set (SISMEMBER cancelled:{triggerId}). If cancelled, skip.
  6. HTTP POST to callback_url with payload. If 2xx → mark FIRED in Cassandra. If timeout/5xx → retry with backoff.
  7. P99 jitter < 1s because the timing wheel operates at 100ms resolution and the sweeper pre-loads triggers 60s before due time

12. Deep Dives

The design above fires triggers. These six are what it takes to fire them on time, once, and without one caller taking down the rest.

Deep Dive 1: Everybody wants to be called back at exactly 14:00:00. Now what?

Bad - the bucketing FR1 chose and FR2 reads: one Cassandra partition per fireAt minute.

  • A typical second holds ~10K triggers. The second at the top of the hour holds a couple of million, because callers ask for round delays from crons that already run on the minute. That is a 200x spike landing on one partition key.
  • Cassandra will warn you about the partition long before it fails, and then it fails in the ugly way: the sweeper’s single-partition read starts taking seconds, during which it is not reading the next bucket either. The jitter target is blown for the hot bucket and for everything behind it.
  • The burst then propagates. Two million triggerIds go into SQS in one go and the dispatcher pool, sized for 10K/sec, sees 200 seconds of work arrive at once while every other caller’s trigger queues behind it.

- the bucketing FR1 chose and FR2 reads: one Cassandra partition per minute.

- sub-shard the bucket. Partition key becomes . The single 14:00 minute is now 64 partitions, evenly distributed, and the sweeper runs 64 parallel reads. The hot partition is gone and the read stays fast.

- three layers, because the hot bucket is three problems wearing one name.

Deep Dive 2: A caller retries register and a dispatcher retries fire. How many callbacks does that produce?

Bad - FR1’s register, which takes the Idempotency-Key and does nothing with it.

  • The caller’s connection drops after we committed but before the 200 reached them. They retry, which is the correct thing for them to do. We write a second row. Seven minutes later the seat hold gets expired twice.
  • The symmetric failure is at the other end: the dispatcher POSTs, gets a 2xx, and dies before writing status = FIRED. SQS redelivers and the next dispatcher reads a row that still says PENDING and fires again. Nothing in FR2 can distinguish “not fired yet” from “fired, ack lost.”
  • Both duplicates are invisible to us and expensive for the caller. This is a trigger service; “call this URL twice” can mean “refund twice.”

- FR1’s register, which takes the and does nothing with it.

- honour the . API stores in Redis with a TTL covering the delay. Repeat requests get the same triggerId.

- combine register-side idempotency with . The dispatcher writes using a Cassandra condition. If two dispatchers race on the same SQS message (visibility-timeout edge case), one wins the conditional write, the other gets a “no-op” and skips the callback. Borrowed from Stripe’s idempotency layer pattern. The caller still has to be ready for at-least-once because the conditional write reduces but doesn’t eliminate duplicates (window between POST returning 2xx and the conditional write).

Deep Dive 3: Where does a 30-day trigger wait?

Bad - FR2’s single hot table, where a 30-day trigger sits in the same keyspace as a 30-second one for a month.

  • The obvious alternative is worse and worth dismissing first: push it to SQS at register time with DelaySeconds=2592000. SQS caps DelaySeconds at 15 minutes, so this does not even compile as a design.
  • What FR2 actually does is keep it in Cassandra, which is right. The problem is what it doesn’t do: nothing ever removes a row. At 10K fires/sec the table grows by 864M rows a day, and FIRED rows outnumber PENDING rows roughly 17,000 to 1 after a month. The sweeper’s partition reads start dragging dead rows off disk, and compaction spends its time rewriting history nobody reads.
  • The long tail makes it worse in a specific way: a trigger registered for one year out keeps its row in the hot table for a year, and there is no way to tell it apart from a trigger that is due in a minute except by reading fireAt.

- FR2’s single hot table, where a 30-day trigger sits in the same keyspace as a 30-second one for a month.

- keep long delays in Cassandra and let the sweeper pick them up when their bucket comes into range. Which is what FR2 built, and it is the right skeleton – the fix is not a different mechanism, it is lifecycle on the rows.

- bucket-aligned so old fired/cancelled rows auto-purge. Set TTL on inserts to so audit data sticks around but the active table stays lean. For super-long delays (> 30 days, e.g., subscription renewal in 1 year), promote to a separate cold table () and have a daily job migrate rows back into the hot table when they’re a day away. Borrowed from Dynein’s “secondary store for far-future” pattern.

Deep Dive 4: One caller’s endpoint hangs for 60 seconds. Why does every other caller stall?

Bad - FR2’s shared dispatcher pool, where every caller’s callback competes for the same threads.

  • Size the pool for 10K fires/sec at a 200ms average callback and you need roughly 2,000 concurrent slots. Now one caller’s endpoint starts hanging to its full 60-second read timeout. Each of their triggers holds a slot 300x longer than a healthy one, so that caller needs only ~33 fires/sec – 0.3% of our traffic – to occupy the entire pool.
  • Everyone else’s triggers now queue in SQS behind a tenant having a bad afternoon. The jitter service level agreement (SLA) fails platform-wide because one customer deployed a bad release. That is the whole failure: a single-tenant outage became a platform outage, and the mechanism was a shared thread pool.

- FR2’s shared dispatcher pool, where every caller’s callback competes for the same threads.

- per-caller dispatcher pools with bulkhead semantics. Each caller gets a slice of the pool capped at, say, 100 concurrent calls. A misbehaving caller can saturate their own slice but not others’.

- circuit breaker per caller (e.g., Resilience4j). Track success rate per ; if >50% errors over the last 30s, open the circuit and fast-fail callbacks to that caller for 60s, dumping them to a per-caller delayed retry SQS. This both protects the dispatcher pool and gives the caller breathing room to recover. Pair with a dashboard surfacing “callers with open circuit” so on-call can reach out. Borrowed from Netflix Hystrix-style isolation.

💡

Deep Dive 5: A cancel lands two seconds before the fire. Who wins?

Bad - FR3’s lazy cancel, read at dequeue.

  • The dispatcher dequeues at T-3s and reads status = PENDING. The caller’s DELETE commits at T-2s and returns 200, so as far as they are concerned the trigger is cancelled. At T+0 the dispatcher POSTs anyway.
  • The caller did everything the API told them to and still got called. There is no number that makes this acceptable: it is a correctness bug in the cancel contract, and the window is however much slack sits between dequeue and POST.
  • Moving the read later shrinks the window but never closes it, because read-then-write is two operations and a cancel can always land between them.

- FR3’s lazy cancel, read at dequeue.

- dispatcher reads at the moment of dispatch, immediately before the POST rather than on dequeue.

- use a Cassandra LWT () to atomically transition right before POST. If the cancel raced and won, the LWT fails and dispatcher skips. This gives us a consistent linearization point at fire time.

Deep Dive 6: What catches a trigger that slips past all five of those?

If a callback fails N times, the trigger lands in a DLQ topic (Kafka). A small operator dashboard surfaces failures by caller. Critically, a reconciler job runs hourly: scans Cassandra for rows with fireAt < now - 1h and status IN (PENDING, IN_FLIGHT) - these are leaks.💡 Reconciliation means periodically comparing what the system should have done against what it did, and repairing the difference. It is the backstop that does not depend on any of the five mechanisms above being correct. Learn more → They get re-pushed to SQS. This is the safety net for any sweeper / leader-election bug. Borrowed from Dynein’s reconciler.

13. Design Self-Audit

  • Single point of failure? Cassandra is multi-DC replicated, SQS is regional with built-in redundancy, Redis cache is tolerable to lose (just rebuild from Cassandra). API and dispatchers are stateless behind a load balancer. ✅
  • Stale reads? Dispatcher LWT on IF status='PENDING' is strongly consistent (Paxos round). The sub-second window between LWT and HTTP POST is the at-least-once gap, accepted. ✅
  • Hot partition? Addressed in Deep Dive 1 with sub-sharding, jitter and the timing wheel. ✅
  • DLQ + reconciliation story? Deep Dive 6. ✅
  • Cost callout for hot tier? SQS at 100K msgs/sec is non-trivial - ~$0.40/M requests, plus delay queue charges. At 100K/s × 86400 = 8.6B msgs/day, that’s ~$3500/day in SQS alone. Worth noting we’d evaluate SQS FIFO vs Redis Streams for cost-sensitive deployments. ✅
  • Search? Not relevant - callers query their own triggers by triggerId, no full-text need.
  • What would a skeptical senior push back on? “Why not just Temporal?” Fair - Temporal solves this and more. Tradeoff: heavier ops, harder to scale to 100K/s of simple delayed triggers without serious tuning. Our scope is the narrow “fire one HTTP callback later” use case, where a purpose-built service is leaner.

14. Core Flows

Flow A: Register + fire (short delay, ≤15 min)

  1. Caller POSTs with delay 120s. API checks idempotency, persists to Cassandra, sends an SQS message with DelaySeconds=120.
  2. After 120s SQS makes the message visible. Dispatcher receives it and looks up the trigger row.
  3. Dispatcher POSTs the payload to the caller’s callbackUrl.
  4. On 2xx, mark FIRED and delete from SQS. Failure path: on 5xx or timeout, dispatcher pushes the message back with exponential ChangeMessageVisibility (e.g., 10s, 30s, 2m, 10m, 30m). After 6 attempts it goes to DLQ.
  5. Non-obvious failure path: dispatcher crashes after POST but before deleting from SQS. SQS visibility timeout expires, another dispatcher receives the message, POSTs again. The caller is expected to dedupe on triggerId - at-least-once is the contract.

Flow B: Long delay (> 15 min)

  1. Trigger lands in Cassandra, partition keyed by floor(fireAt / 1min).
  2. Sweeper for that shard scans bucket = now + 15min every 30 s. Reading 15 min into the future gives slack for sweeper hiccups.
  3. Each row is inserted into the in-process timing wheel.
  4. The wheel ticks; when a slot expires, that triggerId is shipped to SQS with a small DelaySeconds (typically 0–60 s).
  5. Dispatcher path is identical to Flow A from there.
  6. Non-obvious failure path: sweeper leader crashes mid-scan. ZooKeeper detects the session loss, elects a new leader. The new leader rescans the bucket - Cassandra row’s status is still PENDING so it gets re-inserted into the wheel. Possible duplicate fire if the old leader had already pushed to SQS; dedupe on triggerId handles it.

Trigger state machine

PENDING ──register──> in Cassandra
   │
   ├──cancel─────────> CANCELLED (terminal)
   │
   └──dispatcher picks up──> IN_FLIGHT
            │
            ├──2xx ack───> FIRED (terminal)
            └──N retries fail──> FAILED (DLQ, terminal)

15. Final Architecture

How it works end-to-end:

  1. Caller sends trigger request — hits API Gateway, routed to the Trigger API
  2. Idempotency check — API looks up the caller’s key in Redis and, on a repeat, returns the original triggerId rather than creating a second trigger
  3. Trigger persisted — written to Cassandra partitioned by time bucket and sub-shard
  4. Short-delay triggers enqueued — if fire time is <15 min away, pushed directly to SQS
  5. Sweeper hydrates long-delay triggers — leader per shard scans Cassandra buckets approaching due time
  6. Timing wheel fires on schedule — O(1) insert/expire ring buffer pushes messages to SQS when due
  7. Dispatcher delivers callback — consumes from SQS, checks trigger status in Cassandra, POSTs to caller’s callback URL
  8. Failures go to DLQ — permanently-failed deliveries parked in Kafka DLQ for investigation
  9. Reconciler catches leaks — hourly job scans for stuck PENDING triggers and re-enqueues them

Glossary (named components)

  • Sweeper - periodic process that scans Cassandra for triggers due in the next 15 min and pushes them into the in-memory timing wheel. Why it exists: Cassandra is the durable store, but range-scanning it at every tick would be slow; the sweeper hydrates a fast in-memory structure.
  • Timing wheel - ring buffer of time slots (e.g., 1024 slots × 1 ms). Insert is O(1); each tick fires expired slots. Multiple wheels chained give hierarchical resolution (ms → s → min). Borrowed from Kafka Purgatory.
  • Dispatcher - worker that pulls from SQS, reads the trigger row, POSTs to the caller’s callback URL, marks FIRED. Stateless; scale horizontally.
  • Reconciler - hourly safety-net job that finds triggers stuck in PENDING past their fireAt and re-injects them. Catches any leak from sweeper / leader-election bugs.
  • Bucket - Cassandra partition keyed by floor(fireAt / 1min) plus a sub-shard hash. The unit of work the sweeper scans.

Sources

  • Airbnb Dynein - two-tier (SQS + DynamoDB) design, reconciler pattern. Content rephrased for compliance.
  • Kafka Purgatory + Hierarchical Timing Wheels - wheel structure for O(1) timer insert/expire.
  • AWS SQS delay queues docs - 15-min delay primitive.
  • Stripe Idempotency-Key - caller-supplied idempotency pattern.
  • Netflix Maestro overview - sharded execution layer.

Key Technologies

Term What it is
SQS Amazon Simple Queue Service. A managed message queue. You put messages in, consumers take them out. Supports delaying message visibility up to 15 minutes.
Cassandra Distributed NoSQL database. Excellent for time-series/bucketed data. We partition triggers by their fire-time minute for efficient sweeper scans.
Timing Wheel An in-memory data structure (ring buffer) that fires callbacks at precise times. O(1) insert and expiry. Used inside Kafka and Netty.
Sweeper A background job that scans the database for triggers approaching their fire time and moves them into the active queue. Safety net for long delays.
Idempotency Key A unique ID the caller sends with each request. If retried, the server recognizes it’s a duplicate and returns the cached response instead of creating a new trigger.
Circuit Breaker Pattern that stops calling a failing service after N errors. “Opens” the circuit, fast-fails for a cooldown period, then retries. Protects dispatchers from bad callback endpoints.
DLQ (Dead Letter Queue) Where messages go after failing N retries. Allows manual investigation without blocking the main queue.
Reconciler Hourly safety-net job that finds “stuck” triggers (fire time passed but status still PENDING) and re-injects them. Catches bugs in the sweeper or leader election.

What’s Expected at Each Level

This section helps you calibrate your depth. You don’t need to cover everything - just know what’s expected for your level.

Mid-level

Understand the problem - schedule an action to happen at a future time (e.g., “send reminder in 30 min”). Propose a simple DB + polling mechanism. Recognize why polling every second doesn’t scale to millions of triggers - scanning the entire table is O(N) per tick.

Senior

Propose SQS delay queues or hierarchical timing wheels for efficient scheduling. Explain how to shard triggers by time bucket so sweepers only scan a small partition. Discuss idempotent trigger execution and what happens if a trigger fires twice (callers must be idempotent, we provide execution IDs).

Staff+

Address sub-second precision at scale using timing wheels (Kafka-style HashedWheelTimer with O(1) insert and fire). Discuss circuit breaker patterns for downstream callback services, multi-region trigger consistency (what if the primary region fails mid-sweep), and cost comparison of managed SQS vs self-managed timing infrastructure at 10K fires/sec. Cover the reconciler as a safety net for leaked triggers.

🎯 Key Takeaways

  • Timing wheel gives O(1) insert and fire for scheduled events
  • Two-tier: Redis for near-term (<1hr), Cassandra for far-term timers
  • Circuit breaker protects downstream services during cascade failures
  • Lazy cancellation - mark as cancelled, skip on fire (cheaper than deleting from wheel)

  • Dead Letter Queue → — isolates triggers that repeatedly fail to deliver
  • Circuit Breaker → — stops hammering a downstream that’s already unhealthy
  • Retry & Backoff → — re-attempts failed triggers with growing delays
